bacon-or-side-pork-fresh-cooked.title: Bacon or side pork, fresh, cooked

content.title: About
content.content: Bacon or side pork is meat taken from the belly area of a pig. When fresh and cooked, it has a tender texture, a mildly salty aroma, and a soft mouthfeel. It is used in hot dishes, salads, appetizers, and as a garnish for main courses.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional bacon is made from pork belly, but side pork can be prepared in the same way.
Different countries have their own methods: smoking, boiling, or pan‑frying.
Pork is a rich source of high‑quality protein and B‑vitamins, especially B12.
In Russia bacon is often served with potatoes, while in Japan thin slices appear in ramen.
The term “side pork” is sometimes used in culinary schools to refer to slightly leaner cuts than classic bacon.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Bacon provides complete animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains B1, B2, B3, B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains zinc and iron
items.content: These minerals are important for immune health and blood formation.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Makes it suitable for low‑carb diets such as keto.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Bacon is often cured with salt, so people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: A large amount of saturated fat can raise cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Rare, but possible for individuals allergic to pork meat.

items.title: Proper cooking
items.content: Undercooked bacon may harbor harmful bacteria; ensure it is fully cooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bacon can be pan‑fried until crisp, added to soups, stews, salads, or used as a sandwich filling. Cooked slices are also great for cold appetizers when cut thinly.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked bacon in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag for up to 2 months. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration – signs of spoilage.

chicken-leg-drumstick-and-thigh-grilled-.title: Chicken leg, drumstick and thigh, grilled without sauce, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken legs, drumsticks and thighs are dark meat cuts rich in protein and essential micronutrients. Grilled without sauce and with the skin removed, they retain their natural flavor while reducing fat content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark chicken meat contains more iron and zinc than white meat.
Grilling creates a distinctive aroma through Maillard reactions.
These cuts are staples in many world cuisines, from barbecue to Asian marinades.
Skipping the skin cuts the calorie count by roughly 30%.
Proper grilling keeps the meat juicy and tender.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 20 g of high‑quality protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Dark meat supplies iron, which supports hemoglobin formation and energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc aids immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Chicken legs and thighs contain virtually no carbs, making them suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat provides vitamin B6 and niacin, important for metabolic processes.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the meat was previously marinated, sodium levels can be high; plain grilling is preferable.

items.title: Undercooking risk
items.content: Chicken must reach an internal temperature of at least 74 °C to eliminate food‑borne pathogens.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage can lead to salmonella growth; keep refrigerated no more than 2 days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the portion as a main dish, add to salads, wraps, or use as a sandwich filling. Remove the skin before eating to lower fat intake.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked meat in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C, where it remains good for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 74 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Groundhog (720) is a premium plant‑based protein powder designed to support muscle recovery and boost post‑workout energy. The formula is non‑GMO, free from artificial sweeteners and colorants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Combines pea, rice and hemp proteins to deliver a complete amino acid profile.
Each serving provides 20 g of pure protein.
Enriched with digestive enzymes for better nutrient absorption.
Tested to be free of common allergens, including gluten and lactose.
Packaged in recyclable material to reduce environmental impact.

items.title: Supports muscle growth
items.content: A rich blend of essential amino acids promotes muscle protein synthesis after exercise.

items.title: Increases satiety
items.content: High protein content helps you feel fuller longer, which is useful for weight management.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Contains B‑vitamins and zinc that support normal immune function.

items.title: Provides steady energy
items.content: Complex carbs from rice deliver a stable energy release without blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Easy digestion
items.content: Added enzymes (protease, amylase) improve digestion and reduce bloating.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: The product contains pea protein, which may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High fiber content
items.content: Large doses can cause mild gas or stomach discomfort.

items.title: Not suitable for certain kidney conditions
items.content: Due to purine content, people with gout or severe kidney disease should limit intake.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Protein supplements may affect the efficacy of some drugs, such as anticoagulants.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mix one scoop (≈30 g) with 250‑300 ml of water, milk, or a plant‑based beverage. For a richer flavor, add fruit, nuts, or oats. Recommended post‑workout or as a protein snack between meals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place with the package tightly sealed. Keep moisture and direct sunlight away. For storage longer than 6 months, refrigerate.

content.title: About
content.content: A quesadilla is a traditional Mexican dish consisting of a thin corn or wheat tortilla filled with melted cheese and often complemented by meat, vegetables, beans, or sauces. The NFS (New Flavor Series) version uses a special cheese blend that gives a brighter taste and aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Quesadillas originated in Mexico during pre‑Columbian times, originally using corn masa flatbreads.
The word “quesadilla” derives from the Spanish “queso” – cheese.
In the United States, quesadillas gained popularity in the 1990s through fast‑casual Mexican chains.
The NFS variant features a proprietary cheese sauce developed with executive chefs.
Traditionally, quesadillas are cooked on an open flame or a dry skillet without oil.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Cheese and meat or bean fillings provide complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: Cheese is an excellent source of calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Both the tortilla and cheese supply B1, B2, and B12 vitamins that aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Meat and bean additions deliver iron, crucial for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The combination of protein and fat helps maintain a feeling of fullness longer.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Quesadillas, especially those with meat fillings, can be calorie‑dense, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Cheese and sauces often contain significant salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Gluten in wheat tortilla
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should opt for corn tortillas.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the quesadilla on a dry skillet, in the oven, or in a microwave until the tortilla is golden and the cheese melts. Cut into triangles and serve with salsa, guacamole, sour cream, or fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked quesadillas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Freeze in a separate bag at –18 °C, then reheat thoroughly before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Seafood dip is a creamy spread made from seafood such as shrimp, crab meat, and fish, blended with mayonnaise, sour cream, lemon juice, and spices. It has a delicate marine flavor, a slight tang, and a smooth texture, perfect as a sauce for bread, crackers, or vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Originally popular in Japan and the United States, it is a staple at party tables.
Sea salt is often added to enhance the natural taste of the seafood.
Paprika or a pinch of food coloring may be used to give the dip a vibrant hue.
Vegetarian versions replace seafood with mushrooms or tofu, but the classic dip contains real seafood.
Seafood dip is usually served chilled, though a gentle warm‑up can intensify its aroma.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The seafood components provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Shrimp and fish are good sources of omega‑3s, which support heart and vascular health.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is important for nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Seafood dip supplies zinc, selenium, and iodine, which aid immunity and thyroid function.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: When consumed in moderation, the dip fits well into low‑carbohydrate diets.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: People allergic to shrimp, crab, or fish may experience severe reactions after eating the dip.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The creamy base and added salt make the dip relatively salty; individuals with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Short shelf life
items.content: Because it contains fresh seafood, the dip spoils quickly; store it in the refrigerator for no more than 3‑4 days.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Improper storage can lead to bacterial growth and possible food poisoning.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the seafood dip cold with crackers, toast, vegetable sticks, or as a sauce for fish and shellfish dishes. It also works well as a filling for sushi rolls or in sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dip in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration; discard if any signs of spoilage appear.
